title: Hard floor identification: timber, stone, tile, vinyl, concrete
audience: Cleaners who clean hard floors in residential, commercial and turnover work.
learningOutcomes: Identify the common hard floor types by their appearance and feel.
Explain why each type needs a different method and product.
Treat an unknown floor as sensitive until it is identified.

instruction.heading: The main types and how to recognise them
instruction.body:
Five families cover most hard floors you will meet. Timber includes solid boards and engineered boards with a timber top layer. It may be sealed with a film finish, oiled, or left unfinished. Natural stone includes marble, limestone, travertine, slate and granite. Ceramic and porcelain tile are fired clay products, usually glazed, though some are unglazed. Resilient flooring such as vinyl and linoleum is a manufactured sheet or plank, often printed to look like timber or stone. Concrete may be plain, sealed, coloured or polished.

Appearance gives a first view, not a final answer. Timber shows grain and board joints, and it usually feels warm underfoot. Stone shows natural veining or mottled colour, and it feels cool and dense. Glazed tile has a uniform face with grout lines between units. Vinyl often has a repeating print, and it can feel slightly softer than tile. Concrete shows control joints, colour variation and, when dry, a fine powder if it is worked on. Printed vinyl and some manufactured stone look very like the real thing, so a visual check alone is not enough. Look at the joints, the sheen, the wear pattern and the edges, and then confirm with records or a simple test.

instruction.heading: Why the type decides the method
instruction.body:
The material decides which products are safe. Marble, limestone and travertine are calcium-based, and acid reacts with them. The reaction etches the surface and leaves dull marks that cleaning does not remove. This is why an acidic descaler is the wrong choice on a floor that might be stone, however strong the stain looks.

Timber takes up water along the grain, at board edges and through joints. Too much water can swell the boards, lift edges, leave dark stains and allow cupping. Sealed timber resists water better, but the seal still needs a limited moisture method. Finishes on any hard floor can be dissolved by solvents, dulled by alkaline or abrasive products, or stripped by products that are not made for that finish.

Vinyl and linoleum can be marked by some oil-based and solvent products, and by rubber-backed mats or furniture feet left in place. Ceramic and porcelain tile are generally durable, but the grout between them is porous, and abrasive pads can scratch glazed surfaces. Concrete is porous, so stains can soak in, and dry work on the surface can release fine dust. Where that dust may contain crystalline silica, the national guide on silica sets out wet methods and warns against dry sweeping and compressed air (see the safety notes in this lesson).

Before you choose a product, confirm the type and the finish, check the manufacturer's care guidance where it exists, and read the product label and the safety data sheet (SDS). Then test the product on an inconspicuous area and allow it to act for the time the label states before you judge the result.

instruction.heading: Simple identification checks
instruction.body: Start with a visual check under a light held low across the surface. Note the sheen, the pattern, the joints and any worn traffic lanes. Then use a water-drop test in an inconspicuous spot. Place a single drop of clean water on the surface and watch it for a short time. A drop that beads and stays on top suggests a sealed or glazed surface. A drop that darkens or soaks in suggests an unsealed or porous surface. Never use acid, a strong solvent or a harsh abrasive to test a floor. A test that damages the surface gives you a new problem and no answer. Record what you observed and what you could not confirm. A clear record of uncertainty is more useful to the next person than a confident guess.

instruction.heading: When the type is unknown
instruction.body:
If the floor cannot be identified, treat it as sensitive and use the most conservative approved method. In practice this means a pH-neutral or otherwise mild product that your business has approved for unknown surfaces, applied with a damp cloth or microfibre pad. Use no acid, no solvent, no steam and no abrasive pad. Keep the water to a minimum and dry the surface as you go.

Ask the client or supervisor for flooring information. Useful sources include the builder's or installer's records, the strata or property manager's maintenance file, and the manufacturer's care sheet if the flooring brand is known. Do not guess, and do not move to a stronger product until the type is confirmed. Record the floor as unidentified, state the method used, and note the information you requested and from whom.

procedure: Look at the surface, joints, sheen, edges and wear to form a first view of the material.
Ask for the flooring information and check any records or care sheets that are available.
Run a water-drop test in an inconspicuous spot, using clean water only, and record the result.
Confirm the type and finish, or record the floor as unidentified.
If the floor is unidentified, use the most conservative approved method and no acid, solvent, steam or abrasive pad.
Read the product label and SDS, then test the chosen product on an inconspicuous area and wait for the label time before judging it.
Record the floor type, the test result, the product and the method used.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for an acidic descaler on an entrance floor that looks like natural stone. The installer's details are unknown, and the floor has a faint pattern of dull patches.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before any product goes on the floor?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use the acidic descaler. The floor is unidentified and may be natural stone, which acid can etch. Carry out the visual check and a water-drop test on an inconspicuous spot, and record the result. Use the most conservative approved method for an unknown floor. Ask the client or the building manager for the flooring information. If the type is confirmed as natural stone later, choose a stone-compatible product from the approved list. Record the dull patches as found, so they are not blamed on the clean.

workedExamples.situation: A laundry floor of timber boards has a puddle beside the washing machine. The client wants it mopped fully wet so it looks fresh.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you handle the puddle and the request?
workedExamples.reasoning: Remove the standing water first with a dry cloth, then use a damp mop wrung until it is barely wet. Do not flood the boards. Explain that timber takes up water, and that soaking it can swell and stain the boards. Test the approved product on an inconspicuous area, dry the floor promptly, and record the moisture-limited method and the client's request.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved hard floor products, each with its label and SDS on hand.
Soft mops, microfibre pads and non-scratch pads approved for hard floors.
Clean water and a dropper or small spray bottle for the water-drop test.
Torch or work light held low across the surface.
Gloves and eye protection as the SDS requires.
Respiratory protection where dust is generated, as set by the risk assessment and the SDS.

commonErrors.error: Using the same product on every hard floor.
commonErrors.prevention: Identify the type and finish first, then choose the product that matches the approved list for that floor.

commonErrors.error: Using acid on a floor that might be natural stone.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat any unidentified floor as sensitive, and keep acid off floors that are not known to be suitable.

commonErrors.error: Soaking an unsealed timber floor to get it clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a minimal-moisture method on timber, and dry the floor promptly.

commonErrors.error: Testing a floor with a chemical or a harsh abrasive.
commonErrors.prevention: Use clean water for the identification test, and test products only on an inconspicuous area.

commonErrors.error: Recording a guess as a confirmed type.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the observations, the test result and any uncertainty, and mark the floor unidentified until it is confirmed.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Model WHS laws apply in most jurisdictions. They applied from 1 January 2012 in the Commonwealth, the ACT, New South Wales, the Northern Territory and Queensland; from 1 January 2013 in South Australia and Tasmania; and in Western Australia, which passed its adoption on 10 November 2020, from 31 March 2022 (Safe Work Australia, model WHS laws page; no last-updated date shown). The same page states that Victoria is the only jurisdiction that has not implemented the model WHS laws.

A person conducting a business or undertaking must keep a hazardous chemicals register where hazardous chemicals are used, handled or stored. Each listed chemical needs its current SDS, the register must be up to date, and it must be kept at the workplace where workers and others who may be affected can readily reach it. Chemicals that are not classified as hazardous, certain consumer products, and unopened chemicals in transit and stored for 5 days or less are among the exclusions (Safe Work Australia, hazardous chemicals register page; no date shown). The internal chemical reference for the business is not a substitute for this register.

Keep copies of the SDS for chemicals you use, and make sure workers, emergency service workers and anyone else who may be exposed can get at them easily. The page states exceptions for chemicals in transit, unopened retail products and household-quantity consumer products (Safe Work Australia, using safety data sheets page; no date shown).

Concrete and some stone surfaces can release crystalline silica dust when they are dry worked. The national guide for working with silica (February 2022) advises wet methods, low-pressure water, wet sweeping or an approved vacuum, and warns that dry sweeping, compressed air and general-purpose vacuums must not be used to clean dusty surfaces. The guide also states that wet methods alone may not control high-silica dust, and that handheld spray bottles and sponges are not adequate for suppression (Safe Work Australia, national guide for working with silica, February 2022). Whether a specific floor contains silica must be checked against the SDS or the supplier's data.
Product-specific dilution, dwell time and PPE come from the product label and SDS.

qualityStandard: The floor type is identified from the observations and checks, or is recorded as unidentified with the reason.
Where the floor is unidentified, the most conservative approved method is used, with no acid, solvent, steam or abrasive pad.
The product is tested on an inconspicuous area, and the result is recorded before wider use.
Standing water is removed, and the floor is dried promptly after cleaning.
documentationEvidence: Floor identification record with the observations, the water-drop test result and the type or the word unidentified.
Test record for each product used, with the area tested and the result.
Record of the flooring information requested, the person asked and the answer received.
SDS on file for each product used, reachable by workers.
summary: Identify the floor type and finish before you choose a product.
Acid can etch natural stone, and water can swell and stain unsealed timber.
Treat an unknown floor as sensitive, test on an inconspicuous area, and record what you could not confirm.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why can an acidic product damage a floor such as marble?
options: It makes the surface shine more, which clients usually like to see
It has no effect on calcium-based stone at all, so any product is fine
It can etch the stone and leave dull marks that cleaning does not remove
It only affects the grout between the tiles and the edges of the room

knowledgeChecks.question: A floor cannot be identified. What is the correct first step?
options: Use the strongest product to be safe, since it will clean any floor type quickly and fully in one pass
Guess the type from the age of the building, the style of the room and the look of the boards
Treat the floor as sensitive, use the most conservative approved method, and ask for the flooring information
Test the floor with acid in a hidden corner, since acid shows the type of stone clearly and quickly

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is water limited on unsealed timber?
options: Water can swell the timber and cause staining
Water makes timber warmer to walk on in winter
Water removes the grain pattern permanently
Timber does not absorb any water at all
